title: How To Work From Home Without Getting Stressed-Out essed-out/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Drawing on his own six years of working from home while running SCM part-time, Linsin shares productivity habits he says helped teachers suddenly working remotely during the pandemic. He recommends setting strict, shrinking time limits on tasks to trigger Parkinson's Law and sharpen focus, trusting one's instincts rather than overthinking creative or planning decisions, and deliberately handing unresolved problems to the subconscious by stepping fully away from work at a set stop time each day. He frames these as everyday habits to build gradually rather than perfect immediately, promising they reduce work hours while improving output quality. The piece closes with a personal aside about welcoming genuine disagreement in the comments while rejecting mean-spirited posts.
points: Recommends setting strict, shrinking time limits on work tasks to harness Parkinson's Law and boost focus and quality.
Advises trusting instincts over excessive research or overthinking when making creative or planning decisions.
Suggests setting a firm daily stop time and fully disengaging from work to let the subconscious mind process problems.
Frames these techniques as habits to build gradually, not as an all-or-nothing productivity overhaul.
Cites decades of psychological research on the subconscious mind's problem-solving capacity to support stepping away from work.
quotes: It also triggers what is known as Parkinson’s Law, which states: Work tends to expand to fill the time available for its completion.
A good place to start is to cut the amount of minutes you think you need to complete a task by 20 percent and then set a strict work-time limit.
You must trust your instincts and have faith in the ideas and visions that come into your head. If you let them pass or talk yourself out of them, then you’re missing out on your best work.

Psychologists have been writing about the ability of the subconscious to find solutions and move toward goals since the early 1960s. It may seem a bit new-agey and a little out-there, but it really works—with more and more research supporting it.
In the meantime, send tomorrow’s work to your subconscious and feel all that stress you’ve been hanging on to begin melting away.
The only negative is that it can be frustrating to work with others, who may now appear ponderously slow and inefficient.
